newsitem.title: CROATIA: Two candidates secure support to challenge Tudjman.
newsitem.headline: Two candidates secure support to challenge Tudjman.

text.p: Croatia's 75-year-old leader Franjo Tudjman looked well-placed on Monday to win re-election in the first round of next month's presidential vote after only two opposition candidates won the right to get their names on the ballot.

Zdravko Tomac of the Social-Democratic Party (reformed communists), and Vlado Gotovac of the Social Liberals managed to collect by Sunday midnight more than 10,000 signatures needed to qualify for the first round on June 15, the electoral comission said on Monday.

But neither seem to stand a chance of dethroning the president who led Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia, and whose stature and authority within his ruling party and the general population has grown ever since.
Several other potential candidates, including Dobroslav Paraga of the far-right Croatian Party of Rights, failed to collect enough signatures to get their names on the ballot, the commission said.
One of Tudjman's closest aides, Ivic Pasalic, said Tudjman would get between 57 and 62 percent of the vote and win the election in the first round.
"It is realistic for Tudjman to get around 60, Tomac 25 and Gotovac 15 percent, take or leave a few points," political analyst and commentator Davor Gjenero agreed.
"These elections are going to be a plebiscite for Tudjman, and I expect the turnout to be much lower than at the last election," Gjenero said.

The ruling party, Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), won the country-wide poll for municipal bodies and the Upper House of Parliament in April on the back of Tudjman's popularity and failure of the fragmented opposition to agree on co-operation.
Both Tudjman's opponents vowed to change, if elected, the current system in which they argue the president has too much power in comparison with the government and parliament.
Tomac's declared ambition is to force Tudjman into a runoff, while Gotovac's goal is merely to avoid a catastrophic defeat which would end his career as the head of the Social Liberal Party.
Analysts say that Gotovac, a flamboyant former dissident jailed twice by the communist authorities, will have to win at least 22 perent of the vote in order to remain party leader.
This was the result achieved by Gotovac's predecessor and opponent, Drazen Budisa, in the 1992 presidential poll which Tudjman won in the first round with over 55 percent of the vote.

The position of 66-year old Gotovac, the joint candidate of nine centre-left parties, has been considerably weakened by the power struggle within his own party, split over the question whether to co-operate with Tudjman's HDZ or not.
"The voters will ask whether Gotovac is capable of running the country, if he cannot control his own party," Gjenero said.
As a result, Tomac -- a 60-year professor of political science at the Zagreb Univerisity who later turned to practical politics -- has emerged as the most serious challenger to Tudjman.
Tomac's weak spot is his communist past.

Although he never held a senior post in the old Yugoslav regime, he was close to the communist party faction which overturned the republic's popular leadership seeking more autonomy within Yugoslavia back in 1971.

But Tomac has proved his patriotism and won considerable popularity during the war for independence against the Serb-led Yugoslav army in 1991, when he was a deputy prime minister in an all-party "national unity" government.

The Social Democrats claim support among the increasingly impoverished layers of the Croatian population, including pensioners and blue collar workers, who did not profit from the war and the privatisation of the economy.
